title: Montauk Auction Landscape (1879)
summary: In 1879, a court-ordered auction transferred the Montauk proprietors’ holdings to Brooklyn businessman Arthur Benson. Montaukett families still held rights in their homeland. The sale was followed by pressure to leave Indian Fields, broken promises, and a long struggle over land and recognition.

introduction_title: Montauk: a homeland put up for auction
introduction_content: In 1879, a court-ordered auction transferred the Montauk proprietors’ holdings to Brooklyn businessman Arthur Benson. Montaukett families still held rights in their homeland. The sale was followed by pressure to leave Indian Fields, broken promises, and a long struggle over land and recognition.
history_title: From common pasture to auction, displacement and resistance
history_content:
A homeland before it was an auction lot

Montauk is the eastern end of Long Island and a living Montaukett homeland. Indian Fields and North Neck were places of family life, planting, fishing and gathering. English settlers in East Hampton sought grazing land here as their livestock economy expanded. Agreements over land and pasture gradually restricted Montaukett use without ending the community’s presence. McGovern, 2015

The 1703 agreement regulated residence at North Neck and Indian Fields, fenced planting ground, and livestock. Montaukett land use increasingly had to accommodate English grazing. These were restrictions on a people already at home here, not settlement of empty land. McGovern, 2015

Who controlled the land offered for sale?

The Proprietors of Montauk were private shareholders, distinct from the East Hampton Town Trustees who had managed the pasture. A dispute over the trustees’ use of pasture revenue led to litigation; in 1851, a court upheld the proprietors’ title. Their corporate control provided the basis for the later sale. McGovern, 2015 Surviving proprietary records include Native land receipts, court proceedings, grazing lists and Benson’s papers, documenting a long chain of transactions rather than a single moment of land loss. Proprietors of Montauk archive

Why an auction in 1879—and who bought it?

Beginning in 1873, New York businessmen Washington Tyson and Robert M. Grinnell acquired proprietary shares. Grinnell sought a court partition: a way to divide jointly held property or sell it and distribute the proceeds. The resulting auction took place in East Hampton on October 22, 1879. Brooklyn businessman Arthur W. Benson bought the proprietors’ holdings; the historical society’s report records a price of $151,000. Second House report, p. 5

The advertisement offered roughly 11,500 acres, including ponds, expressly subject to Montauk tribal rights and privileges. The auction therefore did not give Benson an unqualified right to remove the Montauketts. He nevertheless pursued private control of a landscape valued for hunting and development. Montauk Library Archives

What happened to Montaukett families?

Benson’s agent Nathaniel Dominy approached people individually to surrender their rights and relocate to Freetown, north of East Hampton village. The Montauk Tribe’s account describes promises that families could return and that Maria Pharaoh would receive continuing support and schooling for her children—promises she later said were not kept. Her 1885 agreement belongs to this history of pressure and unequal bargaining, not a story of a people voluntarily disappearing. Montauk Tribe account

Freetown already had Black and Native residents. Relocation changed where families lived; it did not sever their kinship or Montaukett identity. McGovern’s research follows that continuity across Indian Fields and Freetown. McGovern, 2015 Read the linked Freetown article for more about the community that continued there.

A land struggle became a struggle against erasure

Montauketts challenged the transactions. In 1910, Justice Abel Blackmar rejected their claim and declared the tribe no longer existed, despite the living people pursuing it. The Montauk Tribe’s account explains how racial arguments about intermarriage were used against them. This judicial declaration was not the disappearance of the Montaukett people: descendants have continued community life and advocacy for recognition. Montauk Tribe account

The shaded area on the map shows the broad landscape advertised for auction. It does not mean that every Native right ended in 1879 or that all present-day parcels share one ownership history. The sale, displacement, resistance and continuing community must be read together.

whereintheworld_content:
The approximate area follows the auction map’s eastern peninsula, with an interpretive western line near the Napeague–Fresh Pond transition. The modern shoreline is used for orientation and water is visually excluded even though the advertisement includes ponds. The outline does not resolve small exceptions, station rights, or present ownership. It deliberately does not mark individual homes, burials or archaeological sites.
